title: Gram-Positive Cocci: Staphylococcus and Streptococcus Differentiation and Laboratory Identification
summary: A practical bench-level guide to separating staphylococci from streptococci and then identifying the clinically important species, using colony morphology, catalase, coagulase, hemolysis, bacitracin, optochin, bile esculin, CAMP, PYR, and novobiocin, with attention to reporting and common exam traps.
objectives: Differentiate staphylococci from streptococci using the catalase test and colony morphology.
Apply coagulase, PYR, bacitracin, optochin, CAMP, bile esculin, and novobiocin tests in a logical workup scheme.
Recognize key clinically important gram-positive cocci and report findings consistent with laboratory identification algorithms.
Explain common interferences and false reactions that affect gram-positive coccus identification.

highYield: Catalase positive = staphylococci and micrococci; catalase negative = streptococci and enterococci.
Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase positive (slide clumping factor and tube free coagulase); most other staphylococci are coagulase negative.
Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is beta-hemolytic, bacitracin susceptible, and PYR positive; Group B (S. agalactiae) is beta-hemolytic, CAMP positive, and hippurate hydrolysis positive.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic, optochin susceptible, and bile soluble; viridans streptococci are alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant, and bile esculin negative.
Enterococci are bile esculin positive and grow in 6.5 percent NaCl; they are gamma- or alpha-hemolytic and PYR positive.
quickReview.mnemonic: PYR positive: PYogenes and enteRococcus (both start P and E, both sit on the PYR bench).

deepStudy.introduction: Gram-positive cocci are among the most frequently encountered organisms in clinical specimens, from wound swabs and blood cultures to cerebrospinal fluid and urine. The laboratory algorithm is intentionally simple and hierarchical: first separate staphylococci from streptococci with the catalase test, then branch into coagulase testing for staphylococci or hemolysis-pattern-based testing for streptococci. Mastering this tree is high-yield for both routine bench work and examinations, because most gram-positive coccus questions are simply asking which branch of the tree you are on and which single test moves you to the next node. This lesson walks through the biochemical logic behind each test, the classic colony morphologies that generate your first impression, and the caveats that cause misidentification. Throughout, remember that identification algorithms differ between manual and automated systems, but the underlying biochemical principles remain the same, and any result must be interpreted in the context of specimen source and Gram stain quality.

sections.heading: From Gram stain to catalase: the first fork
sections.body: A well-made Gram stain from a purulent specimen should show gram-positive cocci in clusters (suggesting staphylococci) or chains and pairs (suggesting streptococci or enterococci). Old cultures and stationary-phase staphylococci can appear gram-variable, and over-decolorized streptococci can look gram-negative, so always correlate with plate morphology. On blood agar, staphylococci form medium to large, opaque, often pigmented colonies with beta-hemolysis (S. aureus) or no hemolysis (most coagulase-negative species), while streptococci form smaller, translucent colonies whose hemolysis pattern is the key clue. The catalase test then divides the world: it detects the enzyme catalase that breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, producing visible bubbling. Staphylococci and micrococci are catalase positive; streptococci and enterococci are catalase negative. Use colonies from blood agar, not from media containing red blood cells when possible, because erythrocytes contain catalase and can produce false-positive bubbling. A drop of 3 percent hydrogen peroxide on a glass slide with a visible inoculum is the standard method; a negative control is not routinely needed but the reagent must be fresh and the inoculum adequate. This single test is the most commonly examined fork in the entire gram-positive coccus workup.

sections.heading: Staphylococci: coagulase, latex, and the coagulase-negative group
sections.body: Within the catalase-positive branch, the coagulase test identifies Staphylococcus aureus. Slide coagulase detects bound clumping factor, which agglutinins rabbit plasma directly on a slide; it is rapid but misses clumping-factor-negative S. aureus strains, so a negative slide test must be confirmed by tube coagulase. Tube coagulase detects free coagulase, a coagulase-reacting factor that forms a fibrin clot in plasma, read at 4 hours and again at 18-24 hours; a clot at either reading is positive, while fibrin strands that dislodge when the tube is tipped are not a true clot. Commercial latex agglutination reagents detect protein A and clumping factor simultaneously and are widely used, but they can miss some methicillin-resistant strains and must be validated locally. Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) such as Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus saprophyticus are frequent blood culture contaminants but genuine pathogens in prosthetic device infections and urinary tract infections of young women, respectively. Specimen source and repeated isolation drive the clinical decision to report CoNS. Historically, novobiocin resistance separates S. saprophyticus (resistant) from S. epidermidis (susceptible); note that routine novobiocin testing has been largely supplanted by rapid identification systems, and laboratories must follow current validated procedures.

sections.heading: Streptococci and enterococci: hemolysis as the roadmap
sections.body: In the catalase-negative branch, the hemolysis pattern on sheep blood agar organizes everything. Beta-hemolysis (complete clearing) narrows the field to pyogenes-group streptococci: Streptococcus pyogenes (Lancefield group A) is bacitracin susceptible and PYR positive, while Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) is bacitracin resistant, CAMP positive, and hippurate positive. The CAMP test uses the synergistic hemolysis between the CAMP factor of group B streptococcus and staphylococcal beta-lysin streaked perpendicular to each other; an arrowhead zone of enhanced clearing is positive. PYR (L-pyrrolidonyl arylamidase) hydrolysis produces a red color with the developer reagent and is positive for S. pyogenes and enterococci, making it the tiebreaker when bacitracin results are ambiguous. Alpha-hemolysis (partial greening) points to Streptococcus pneumoniae or the viridans group. Pneumococci are optochin susceptible and bile soluble (lysed by sodium desoxycholate), and they characteristically appear as lancet-shaped diplococci; optochin disks must be read on sheep blood agar after overnight incubation in 5 percent carbon dioxide. Viridans streptococci resist optochin and are bile esculin negative. Gamma-hemolysis (no clearing) plus bile esculin hydrolysis and growth in 6.5 percent NaCl confirms Enterococcus, an organism intrinsically tolerant of bile and salt and now commonly classified as Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium by automated systems.

sections.heading: Pitfalls, mixed cultures, and reporting language
sections.body: Mixed staphylococcal-streptococcal wounds are common; report both organisms with a comment about mixed flora when the culture is not sterile-site, rather than forcing a single identification. Catalase false positives occur when colonies are taken from blood-containing media, and false negatives occur with old hydrogen peroxide. Slide coagulase can be falsely negative, so never report S. aureus from a slide test alone without the required confirmation in your laboratory's procedure. S. pneumoniae autolyses in older cultures and can appear as gram-negative ghosts; subculture promptly to a fresh blood agar plate. Enterococci may show alpha-hemolysis and be mistaken for viridans streptococci until bile esculin and salt broth testing are done. Streptococcus anginosus group organisms can show variable hemolysis and produce abscesses with a sweet odor, a classic practical detail. When reporting, include the identification at the level your validation supports, note susceptibility testing when clinically indicated, and use comments such as 'mixed culture, correlate with Gram stain and clinical findings' where appropriate. Exam questions often test the single discordant test result, so rehearse the tree until each node is automatic: catalase, then coagulase, then hemolysis, then the targeted confirmatory test.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: S. aureus causes skin and soft-tissue infections, bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and toxin-mediated disease; methicillin resistance (MRSA) changes empiric therapy and infection control. Coagulase-negative staphylococci are leading causes of prosthetic valve, joint, and catheter-related infections. S. pyogenes causes pharyngitis, impetigo, scarlet fever, and invasive disease with streptococcal toxic shock; S. agalactiae is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, so prenatal screening matters. S. pneumoniae is the classic community-acquired pneumonia and meningitis pathogen. Enterococci cause urinary tract infections, endocarditis, and nosocomial infections, with vancomycin resistance (VRE) a major control problem. Accurate differentiation directly shapes empiric antibiotic choices and infection-control decisions.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Interpret every identification in light of specimen source and Gram stain quality: a single coagulase-negative staphylococcus from one blood culture set is often a contaminant, while the same organism from two sets plus prosthetic material is clinically significant. Beta-hemolysis must be read with transmitted light on sheep blood agar; horse blood agar can mask hemolysis. Zone diameters for bacitracin and optochin must follow current CLSI-aligned procedures because disk content and breakpoints can change. Always document confirmatory test results (for example, tube coagulase at 4 and 18-24 hours) rather than reporting preliminary presumptive findings as final. When automated identification scores are low, repeat the Gram stain, subculture for purity, and perform the classic biochemical panel before reporting. Reference intervals do not apply to qualitative cultures; report organism identification and susceptibilities per your laboratory's validated algorithm.

examTraps: A negative slide coagulase does not exclude S. aureus; clumping-factor-negative strains exist and require tube coagulase or latex confirmation.
PYR positivity does not mean group A streptococcus alone - enterococci are also PYR positive, so you must combine PYR with hemolysis and bile esculin results.
Reading optochin on the wrong medium or after the wrong incubation atmosphere gives false susceptibility; use sheep blood agar with 5 percent carbon dioxide per current procedure.
Erythrocytes contain catalase, so picking colonies directly from blood agar for catalase can give false-positive bubbling if the inoculum carries red cells.

memoryHooks.text: Catalase positive = Staph (think: Staph has a 'shield' of catalase bubbles). Beta-hemolysis + PYR positive = pyogenes; beta-hemolysis + CAMP positive = agalactiae.
memoryHooks.funny: Mimi the cat: 'Ang staph, marunong mag-bubble bath (catalase positive)! Ang strep? Walang bubbles, kaya chains of sadness lang.'

memoryHooks.text: Bile esculin positive plus growth in 6.5 percent NaCl = Enterococcus, the salt-and-bile champion.
